title: Polynomial-size closure of d-DNNF under negation
formal:
Do constants \(c>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) exist such that, for every finite variable set \(X\) and every d-DNNF circuit \(C\) over \(X\), there is a d-DNNF circuit \(D\) over \(X\) with
\[s(D)\le c\bigl(s(C)+1\bigr)^k\quad\text{and}\quad\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\ f_D(a)=1-f_C(a)?\]
The constants are universal: they cannot depend on \(X\), \(C\) or its Boolean function. No algorithm, uniformity or bound on the time needed to find \(D\) is required. Its internal decompositions may differ from those of \(C\), with no global variable-tree restriction on either circuit.
definitions:
A negation-normal-form Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output gate. A leaf is a constant \(0\) or \(1\), or a literal \(x\) or \(\neg x\) for a variable in a finite set \(X\). Each internal gate is AND or OR with a finite nonempty input list. Arbitrary fan-in and sharing of subcircuits are allowed, and every input occurrence counts as an edge. Evaluation on an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\) uses the ordinary Boolean operations. There are no other negation gates. Constants suffice when \(X\) is empty.

For a gate \(g\), let \(\operatorname{var}(g)\) be the variables appearing in the literals reachable by following its input edges. Decomposability requires that the input subcircuits of each AND gate have pairwise disjoint such variable sets. Determinism requires that, for every OR gate, no assignment to \(X\) makes two distinct input occurrences true simultaneously. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions at every gate. Determinism is a semantic mutual-exclusion property; it is not a restriction to gates that branch on a single variable.

Write \(f_C(a)\) for the output of circuit \(C\) and \(s(C)=|V(C)|+|E(C)|\) for its size, including leaves and all wires. Unused variables in \(X\) do not affect evaluation. Smoothness, which would require all inputs of an OR gate to mention the same variables, is not assumed. There is also no common tree organizing the variable splits of all conjunction gates. Thus the target uses general d-DNNFs, not only the smaller class of structured d-DNNFs. When two circuits are compared, their variable names denote the same coordinates of a common assignment; a missing coordinate is simply ignored by that circuit.

The output uses only variables of \(X\), interpreted on the same coordinates, with no auxiliary variables or existential projection. It need not mention every variable. The size counts the complete circuit rather than an implicit description or an oracle for evaluating it. The target is nonconstructive representational closure with polynomial overhead, not closure as a set of Boolean functions alone.

The exact negation of the claim is that for every \(c>0\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), some finite \(X\) and some d-DNNF \(C\) have the property that every d-DNNF \(D\) computing its complement satisfies \(s(D)>c(s(C)+1)^k\). This need not be witnessed by one fixed input circuit defeating all polynomials, or by an efficiently constructible family. A uniform polynomial-time complementing algorithm would imply the size bound; the converse is not part of this statement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal polynomial-size closure statement. A proof must supply universal constants and establish a complement representation satisfying the bound for every input circuit. A refutation must establish the quantified superpolynomial obstruction for general output d-DNNFs. A lower bound that only excludes structured outputs, a particular decomposition or a particular algorithm is insufficient. Computational difficulty in finding a complement alone also does not refute existence of a small complement.
why: This question isolates whether Boolean negation inherently destroys the succinctness of a central tractable representation. It separates a representational obstruction from the algorithmic difficulty of discovering a representation. A negative answer would exhibit a fundamental asymmetry between compact descriptions of a set of assignments and its complement; a positive answer would establish polynomial-size robustness under negation.

importance.reason: A central representational-closure question in knowledge compilation that separates succinctness from the cost of performing a logical operation.

context_blocks.text: The source question explicitly separates efficient complementation from existence of a small complement. Every Boolean complement has some d-DNNF representation; the issue is a polynomial bound, and for the computational version a uniform algorithm achieving one.

The knowledge-compilation map treats negation as a transformation with an output representation, separately from queries such as counting satisfying assignments or comparing functions. Its d-DNNF negation entry is unresolved.

Vinall-Smeeth proves a superpolynomial complement-size lower bound when the output must remain structured, even without output determinism. The source leaves unstructured d-DNNF complementation open: removing the global variable-tree restriction changes the target of the lower bound.

The 2026 probabilistic-word paper connects complement gates in tractable circuit representations to the unresolved succinctness question for d-DNNFs. This is evidence of an additional counting-language connection, not a general complement construction or lower bound.

progress.text: The structured-class separation is first posted as arXiv:2402.04832 and later published at IJCAI 2024; its output restriction leaves the general question open.
The STACS paper explicitly retains d-DNNF complementation as an open question in its conclusion.

sentences: The question asks whether every d-DNNF has a polynomial-size d-DNNF representing its Boolean complement.
One polynomial must bound the size increase for every circuit and every finite variable set.
The complement may use entirely different decompositions, provided that decomposability and determinism are retained.
No efficient procedure for finding the complement is required in this representational question.
The published failure of closure for structured circuits does not settle closure for general d-DNNFs.
